| regression holding call count fixed prices **+7.0% [1.9, 13.2]** tax on merely having made the call, and one call at **1.61 messages**, not 1 | **removing 94 calls removes ~151 messages, not 94** |
| no static feature predicts a no-op call (best AUC 0.553 at 28% base rate) | selective skipping is impossible; pre-delivery must be universal |
| of 188 pre-edit greps the payload missed, **2 (1.1%)** named a literal in the agent's query but not the issue | **the retrieval objection is already measured away** |

That last row kills the main risk I put on R-A in the plan. I priced it at +5.9% assuming the payload would be worse because prefetched retrieval scores lower on gold-visible@5. But the agent's own query adds ~1% over the issue text, and the earlier strike was on retrieval, not tokens.

Removing an eg-only instruction can't bias toward eg — it strictly reduces the asymmetry.

    per=collections.Counter(); cnt=collections.Counter(); nsess=0; tot_persist=0
    for cj in glob.glob(f"results/{tag}/{arm}/*/cc_out.json"):
        try: j=json.load(open(cj))
        except: continue
        if j.get("subtype")!="success": continue

        if not(os.path.exists(p) and os.path.getsize(p)>0): continue

        for line in open(tf,errors="ignore"):
            try: m=json.loads(line)

            msg=m.get("message") or {}
            if msg.get("role")=="assistant":

That kills the R-B reframing too, and identifies what the tool is actually doing.

**Exploration calls are already cheap: median 732 B**, p90 3.6 KB, only 1.3% over 8 KB. The graph's own output has a **median of 1,124 B — larger than a median grep.** A graph-backed grep would *add* bytes. R-B is dead on both metrics, not just the one I tested.

Exploration's 47% share comes from *volume* (1,206 calls), not size. The concentrated cost is elsewhere:

| | baseline | eg |
|---|---|---|
| whole-file reads | 119 | **105** |
| median size | 5,125 B | **4,081 B** |
| calls >8 KB | 39 (32.8%) | **25 (23.8%)** |
| share of whole-file bytes in those | 70.9% | **60.4%** |
| range reads | 121 | **133** |

**This is the tool's real mechanism, and it's the one place it works:** eg converts whole-file reads into range reads — 14 fewer whole-file, 12 more ranged, median size down 20%, and the expensive >8 KB tail cut from 39 calls to 25. That's the 21% capture of the single most concentrated context category, and it is essentially the entire +1.35%.

It also bounds the remaining upside: pushing whole-file 105 → 40 (converting to ranges) is worth ≈ **−3.6M of 38.5M = +9.4%**. With R-A's +4.8–6.9% that's **+14–16%** — the sixth independent derivation landing in the same band.

Two levers survive the hour, both fair, neither reaching 35%:

| lever | status | worth |
|---|---|---|
| **R-A** zero-toll delivery | **built, offline-gated, committed `b669a57b`** | +4.8% to +6.9% |
| **R-D** whole-file → range conversion | mechanism identified, not built | ≈ +9% |

# entire-graph — the finalized plan

**2026-08-08.** Supersedes `PLAN-TO-35PCT.md` and `EG-ROUTE-TO-35.md`. Everything below is
measured on rep50 (49 gated pairs, Opus, SWE-bench Multilingual) unless marked projection.
Sign convention: **positive = the graph arm saved tokens.**

---

## 1. The metric is context, not messages

    tokens +1.35%  =  turns −1.42%  +  tokens/turn +2.74%

The eg arm spends **38 more turns** and still wins, so the saving is not a message saving.
**cache_read is 95.5% of all tokens** (cache_creation 3.0%, output 1.5%). This is a context-size
problem. The independent prefetch measurement at `run_3arm.sh:482` found the same thing on a
different cell (30,302 → 29,334 tok/turn, −3.2%).

Variance decomposition of the paired log token ratio: turns 34.2%, tokens/turn 26.0%, covariance
39.8% (entangled, corr +0.668). Neither side dominates alone.

**Accounting unit used throughout:** a tool result injected at turn *i* is re-charged on every
later turn, so its cost is `(bytes ÷ 4) × turns-remaining` — "persist-tokens".

---

## 2. The complete budget

Baseline total: **38.6M persist-tokens**. eg: 38.5M. **The tool is context-neutral (+0.2%).**

| category | baseline | share | eg | captured |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **source-code exploration** | 10.48M | 27.2% | 8.25M | **21%** |
| **whole-file `Read`** | 11.67M | 30.3% | 9.20M | **21%** |
| test exploration | 1.94M | 5.0% | 2.87M | **−48%** |
| range `Read` | 3.60M | 9.3% | 4.40M | −22% |
| harness runs | 4.30M | 11.2% | 3.70M | 14% |
| log / scratch output | 1.95M | 5.1% | 2.36M | not addressable |
| environment / deps | 0.76M | 2.0% | 0.62M | not addressable |
| build manifests | 0.31M | 0.8% | 0.34M | not addressable |
| graph calls | 0 | — | 1.70M | cost |

**Graph-addressable = source exploration + whole-file reads + tests = 24.1M of 38.6M (62.4%).**
eg captures 3.78M gross, adds 3.10M (graph calls 1.7M, range reads +0.8M, other +0.6M), so
**net 0.68M = 1.8% ≈ the observed +1.35%.** The model reconciles to the measurement.

Two structural facts that kill obvious ideas:

- **Exploration calls are already cheap** — median **732 B**, p90 3.6 KB, 1.3% over 8 KB. Its 47%
  share is *volume* (1,206 calls), not size. The graph's own output has a median of **1,124 B**,
  larger than a median grep, so a graph-backed grep would add bytes. (Kills R-B.)
- **Whole-file reads are the opposite** — 119 calls, median 5,125 B, p90 20 KB; 39 calls carry
  70.9% of the bytes. 98k persist-tokens each, **7× an exploration call**.

---

## 3. Why the uncaptured cost is uncaptured — the decisive split

For every remaining call, was what it asked for already in the delivered payload?

**Whole-file reads still made by eg (105 calls, 9.2M):**

| cause | calls | share of cost |
|---|---|---|
| **c) file was in the payload WITH its body** | 24 | **42.3%** |
| no payload logged (detector bug, §6.1) | 36 | 36.0% |
| a) file never in the payload | 42 | 21.1% |
| b) in payload as a locator only | 3 | 0.5% |

**Source-code exploration still done by eg (319 calls with a logged payload, 8.09M):**

| cause | calls | share of cost |
|---|---|---|
| **coverage — no query term in payload** | 117 | **26.9%** |
| **partial coverage — some terms** | 96 | **42.2%** |
| ignored payload — all terms delivered | 57 | 15.9% |
| no identifier in the query | 49 | 15.0% |

**These point in opposite directions and that is the whole finding.**
Whole-file reads are dominated by the agent re-opening a file it was already given in full —
**not tool-fixable**, and the same wall as 0/66 verb adoption. Source exploration is dominated by
**coverage (69.1%)** — the payload genuinely did not contain what the agent asked for next, and
the misses are specific symbol lookups the graph should own (`replaceGt|replaceLt|replaceGte`,
`def get_deprecation_message`, `path_hooks|def _install`).

---

## 4. The ceiling, computed from the budget

| | persist-tokens | as % of 38.6M |
|---|---|---|
| graph-addressable pool | 24.1M | 62.4% |
| …of which coverage-fixable | ~7.5M | **19.4%** |
| …of which ignored-payload (needs an instruction) | ~5.2M | 13.5% |
| …of which already captured | 3.78M | 9.8% |
| payload cost to widen coverage (projection) | −2 to −3M | −5 to −8% |

**Coverage work, delivered perfectly and priced honestly: ≈ +12%.**
**R-A (remove the call toll): +4.8% to +6.9%** — computed directly, not modelled.
**Together: +15% to +19%.**

35% would require capturing ~65–70% of the addressable pool at near-zero payload cost. The
ignored-payload share alone (13.5%) is out of reach without an instruction, and an instruction
telling the agent to re-read less would help a no-tool arm equally — **which is exactly what the
withdrawn −35% contained** (removing two such sentences moved that cell from −14.9% to +9.1%).

**Seven independent derivations, all landing in the same band:**

| route | ceiling |
|---|---|
| perfect loser repair (= the lift pool, exact) | **+21.21%** |
| best fair cell ever measured (opus xhigh, n=26) | **+17.21%** |
| coverage + R-A, from the context budget | **+15% to +19%** |
| R-A + R-B + current, message model | ≈ +17% |
| expensive-baseline tercile (78% of token mass) | +8.07% |
| hand-classified post-edit waste (763 calls) | +2.67% to +4.57% |
| directly addressable post-edit surface | +2.3% |

> **35% is not reachable on a fair measurement. The honest number is +15% to +21%.**

---

## 5. What to do, in order

### 5.1 SHIP — R-A, zero-toll delivery *(built, gated, committed `b669a57b`)*

`EG_PREFETCH=1` has always injected the payload into turn 0 **and** let the agent's residual
search re-derive it at full price (~5 s + an index build) — delivered twice, paid for once at
full price. That is why every prefetch attempt measured null. `EG_PRESEARCH` makes the residual
call an echo.

Offline gate passed, $0: echo byte-identical to the prompt block; **0.02 s vs 5.21 s**; missing
payload errors rather than silently re-querying; real search unaffected when unset; other verbs
unaffected; export proven eg-only by block matching (line 704, inside `arm = eg` 446–939 and the
`EG_PREFETCH` gate at 498).

Worth **+4.8% to +6.9%**. Fair without qualification: the eg prompt gains tool output and *loses*
an instruction. **Next step: run it as a paired cell.**

### 5.2 BUILD — coverage of the agent's *next* query

Target the 69.1% coverage share of source exploration. The failing queries are specific symbol
lookups. This is the one pool that is genuinely tool-fixable.

Do **not** measure it with gold-file coverage — that metric is anti-correlated with winning
(gold at rank 1: losers 6/8, winners 2/5) and eleven payload metrics have died on it. Measure it
as: *of the identifiers the agent greps for after receiving the payload, what fraction were in
the payload?* Today that is **30.9%** (all-terms 15.9% + partial credit). Gate on raising it.

Price the payload growth against the capture — a wider payload costs persist-tokens too, and at
median 1,124 B the graph's output is not free.

### 5.3 DO NOT BUILD

- **R-B, graph-backed grep** — dead twice: 38.9% interception, and graph output is *larger* than
  a median grep.
- **Anything gated on an agent-initiated call** — 0/66 (`impact` 0/49, `changed` 0/5, `--path`
  0/12). A fourth verb will measure zero.
- **Whole-file-read suppression** — 42.3% of the remaining cost is the agent re-opening a file it
  already has in full. Only an instruction fixes that, and that instruction is unfair.
- The twelve struck levers in §6.

---

## 6. Struck — measured, do not re-propose

1. Eleven payload-quality metrics (completeness, gold coverage, byte width, rank) — all 0.
2. **Complete-symbol payload density** — corr with token saving **−0.170**; the 3+ group measures
   **−4.28%** against +1.35% overall. *(Twelfth.)*
3. Retrieval/ranking quality — anti-correlated (gold at rank 1: losers 6/8 vs winners 2/5).
4. Session-length routing · language/repo gating · confidence gating (abstention worse).
5. Per-loser repair — +0.0 pt; ~93% of losers flip sign between cells.
6. Locate-call reduction as a token lever — corr +0.188 over 10 cells.
7. Raising the turn cap — both arms grow proportionally.
8. `EG_VERIFY_MODE=noworld` — +35.1% **worse**.
9. Symmetric frugality clamp — net-negative: in the winners it is the *baseline* that flails
   (lombok baseline `javac`×70 vs eg ×23), so a shared clamp hands savings to the baseline.
10. More graph calls — G3: 1.9 → 3.1 calls, displacement 0.96 → 0.76.
11. Post-edit delivery gated on an agent-initiated call — G2 measured **−12.19%**, rider fired 0/5.
12. Any new verb in the affordance tail — 0/66.

### 6.1 Open defects — fix before the next cell

1. **`EMPTY PAYLOAD` detector is broken.** Fires on sessions holding 7,757 payload bytes and 3
   graph calls (3× in G3). It also blanks 36 of 105 whole-file reads (36% of that cost) from
   classification. Any payload forensics is unreliable until it is fixed.
2. **Gate admits junk patches** — `carbon-2981` baseline patch was 371,308 B (vendor/build
   output) and passed as success. Add a symmetric size/content bound.
3. **VMs A and B are spot and were preempted** — Gemini 300 frozen at n=207, 52 rep30 sessions
   stranded. Move long cells to non-preemptible (E/F) or checkpoint.
4. **`.entire/graph-agent.md` fairness landmine** — carries arm-asymmetric methodology and is
   `@`-included into `CLAUDE.md`. It did *not* leak into rep50 (`--safe-mode`, 0 injected files
   verified both arms), but any cell run without `--safe-mode` is invalid on arrival. Add a
   preflight assertion rather than relying on the flag.

---

## 7. Corrections issued this session

Recorded so they are not re-derived, and because two were mine.

1. **eg does NOT verify more than the baseline — it verifies less** (545 vs 576 harness runs;
   post-edit 384 vs 422). The opposite claim came from the 8 worst *losers*, a set selected on
   the outcome. Over-verification is what a losing session looks like in either arm; the biggest
   win, `lombok-3674` (+71.0%), is the *baseline* running `javac` 70× against eg's 23.
2. **First-word Bash classification undercounted exploration by 41%** (855 → 1,206 baseline).
   `wc -l f && cat f` and `gem list | grep …` were filed as "other bash". Corrected, the graph
   costs **37 more messages than it removes**, and the saving is entirely context density.
3. **Perfect loser repair caps at +21.21%**, exactly — it is the sum of the lift pool, not an
   estimate. Loser repair cannot reach 35% by definition.
4. The **+35.06%** target was an arithmetic artifact (applying the winner group's eg/base ratio,
   earned on 2.64M-median baselines, to 0.99M baselines where the waste does not exist).
   Retracted.

The hour's work is finalized and verified. `devenv/EG-FINAL-PLAN.md`.

## What the verification caught

I nearly shipped a plan claiming the context model "reconciles to the measurement." It doesn't — the persist-token model predicts **+2.51%** against a measured **+1.35%**, over-predicting by **~1.9×**. Every projection built on it now carries a **×0.54 calibration**, which pulled my own coverage estimate from +12% down to **+7%**.

## The finalized position

**The metric is context, not messages.** `tokens +1.35% = turns −1.42% + tok/turn +2.74%` — eg spends 38 *more* turns and still wins. cache_read is 95.5% of all tokens.

**The complete budget** (38.6M persist-tokens, baseline):

| category | share | eg captures |
|---|---|---|
| whole-file `Read` | 30.3% | 21% |
| source-code exploration | 27.2% | 21% |
| harness · tests · ranges · logs · env · manifests | 42.5% | ~0 |

Graph-addressable = **62.4% raw, 33.7% calibrated**. So even capturing the *entire* addressable surface at zero payload cost lands at ~34% — and 7.2% of that is ignored-payload no tool change reaches.

**The decisive split — and the two pools point opposite ways:**

- **Whole-file reads: 42.3% of remaining cost is the agent re-opening a file the payload already gave it in full.** Not tool-fixable. Same wall as 0/66 verb adoption.
- **Source exploration: 69.1% is a genuine coverage gap** — the misses are specific symbol lookups (`replaceGt|replaceLt|replaceGte`, `def get_deprecation_message`). This is the one genuinely fixable pool.

## The answer on 35%

**Not reachable on a fair measurement.** Seven independent derivations, and the two built this hour from the context budget sit at the *bottom* of the band:

| route | ceiling |
|---|---|
| perfect loser repair (exact — the lift pool) | +21.21% |
| best fair cell ever measured | +17.21% |
| **calibrated context budget: coverage + R-A** | **+12% to +14%** |

Reaching 35% requires an instruction telling the agent to explore and re-read less — which helps a no-tool arm equally, and is precisely what the withdrawn −35% contained.

## What to do

1. **Ship R-A** — built, offline-gated, committed `b669a57b`. Fixes a real defect: prefetch injected the payload into turn 0 *and* let the agent re-derive it at full price. Worth **+4.8–6.9%**, fair without qualification. Ready to run as a cell.
2. **Build next-query coverage** — gate on "fraction of identifiers the agent greps for that were in the payload," today **30.9%**. Not gold-file coverage, which is anti-correlated with winning. Worth ~**+7%**.
3. **Don't build**: R-B (dead twice), any fourth tail verb (0/66), whole-file suppression (42.3% is ignored payload).

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:

- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. ## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

# entire-graph on Opus — what the data says, and the only plan that survives it

## Context

The goal set for this work is **35% token savings on rep50, fairly measured, on Opus**. This plan
exists because that target is now refuted by the data, and continuing to aim at it would mean
either fabricating it or measuring something else and calling it that. What follows is the
evidence, the loser/winner analysis requested, and the plan that is actually supported.

All numbers: rep50, Opus/max, 49 gated pairs, SWE-bench Multilingual.
Sign convention: **positive = the graph arm saved tokens.**

---

## 1. Where Opus actually stands

| | value |
|---|---|
| headline | **+1.35%** |
| t-statistic | **−0.17 — indistinguishable from zero** |
| median | −4.2% |
| wins | 24 / 49 |
| paired sd (log-ratio) | 0.494 |
| n to *demonstrate* +1.35% | **12,900 pairs ≈ $78,491** |
| n to demonstrate +6% | 499 pairs ≈ $3,972 |
| n to demonstrate 35% | **11 pairs ≈ $88** |

**35% would have been the cheapest result in the project to prove.** It is not provable because
it is not there. Every robust estimator drives the headline to zero or below — winsorised 20/80
**−0.26%**, dropping the 3 most extreme pairs **−6.19%** — so the positive sign is tail-carried.

---

## 2. Loser analysis (requested)

**Drag −19.86 pts across 25 instances; top five carry −11.42 (57%).**

Group sums, eg minus baseline:

| | losers (25) | winners (24) |
|---|---|---|
| turns | **+296** | −258 |
| **pre-edit exploration** | **−46** | **−58** |
| post-edit exploration | **+159** | −81 |
| post-edit harness | **+50** | −88 |
| edits | +42 | −25 |
| graph calls | 44 (43 pre) | 50 (48 pre) |

**The single most important line is pre-edit exploration: the graph works in BOTH groups
(−46 / −58).** Localization is not what separates them. The entire divergence is post-edit, where
**91 of 94 graph calls never happen** — 42/49 sessions make no graph call after their first edit.

Worst five, with the pattern visible per-instance:

| instance | pts | tok | eg/base turns | eg/base expl | eg/base harness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bat-1892` | −2.81 | −79.8% | 100/65 | 44/18 | 23/14 |
| `valkey-790` | −2.72 | −127.4% | 93/54 | 57/34 | 20/11 |
| `ansible-395e` | −2.58 | −68.1% | 116/91 | 48/38 | 9/5 |
| `prometheus-9248` | −1.68 | −74.6% | 110/68 | 68/38 | 9/8 |
| `tokio-4867` | −1.63 | −114.4% | 69/38 | 26/10 | 25/17 |

**Correlates with token saving, ranked:**

| | r |
|---|---|
| Δ harness runs | **−0.612** |
| Δ exploration eliminated | +0.485 |
| Δ repeat edits to same file | −0.457 |
| Δ edit calls | −0.449 |
| **Δ harness ENV failures** | **−0.442** |
| Δ throwaway scripts run | −0.350 |
| Δ first-edit turn | −0.342 |

**Mechanism:** losers run verification that fails on the *environment* rather than the patch
(eg 102 vs base 80 in the loser group), then improvise throwaway harnesses (+16) and re-explore
to repair them (+159 post-edit exploration). Winners show the exact mirror: **−45 env failures,
−48 throwaway scripts, −88 harness runs**. This is the ledger's §1.3 lever, independently
reproduced here.

---

## 3. Winner analysis — what must not regress

**Lift +21.21 pts across 24 instances. `lombok-3674` alone is +6.09 pts = 29% of ALL lift.**

| instance | pts | eg/base turns | eg/base harness |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lombok-3674` | **+6.09** | 67/122 | **23/70** |
| `fmt-2457` | +2.18 | 38/67 | 12/13 |
| `qutebrowser-c580` | +1.89 | 88/105 | 23/33 |
| `vuejs-11739` | +1.35 | 70/80 | 24/19 |
| `redis-11510` | +1.29 | 34/56 | 3/12 |

**Winners win because the BASELINE flails and eg converges** — lombok's baseline ran `javac`
**70 times** against eg's 23. eg is not doing something clever; it is failing to blow up.

**Two consequences that constrain every proposal below:**

1. **A symmetric frugality clamp is net-negative.** Suppressing over-verification helps the
   baseline more than eg in exactly the instances eg currently wins. Already modelled; do not
   ship one.
2. **Any intervention that adds post-edit content risks converting a winner into a loser**, since
   winners win by *doing less* after the first edit. Winner protection is therefore not a
   formality — it is the main risk.

---

## 4. What is already closed (do not rebuild)

| route | verdict |
|---|---|
| new verb in the affordance tail | **0/66 adoption** (`impact` 0/49, `changed` 0/5, `--path` 0/12) |
| post-edit rider (G2) | **−12.19%**, fired 0/5 |
| displacement via better verbs (G3) | ratio **0.76** vs 0.96 baseline — went backwards |
| graph-backed grep | 38.9% interception ceiling; graph output (1,124 B median) is *larger* than a median grep (732 B) |
| next-query coverage | only 40.4% of missed identifiers are graph symbols; of those 89% stay missing at 4× payload budget |
| payload quality | 12 metrics dead, incl. complete-symbol density (r = **−0.170**) |
| retrieval/ranking | anti-correlated — gold-at-rank-1 sessions lost more often |
| tail-risk endpoint | arms blow up at identical rates (22.4% vs 20.4%); n=6,338 to resolve |

---

## 5. The plan

### 5.1 Accept the honest target

**Stop targeting 35% on Opus.** Target **loser repair**, whose exact ceiling is the lift pool:
**+21.21%** if every losing instance were made precisely neutral. That is arithmetic, not
projection. Reaching it requires eliminating the drag pool entirely; a realistic fraction is
worth +5–10%.

### 5.2 Build: VERIFY runnability probe *(primary — targets the measured mechanism)*

**Files:** `internal/sem/search_verify.go` (derivation + probe), `internal/cli/search.go`
(VERIFY block emission).

Today the only check is `exec.LookPath` on the runner (`search_verify.go:1526`) — it confirms
`pytest` exists, never that the derived command *runs*. Add a **collect-only probe** before
emitting: `pytest --collect-only -q`, `go test -run XXX -count=0`, `cargo test --no-run`,
`mvn -q -DskipTests compile`. On failure, drop to the next rung rather than emitting a command
that will fail on the environment.

Also raise VERIFY coverage — it appears in only **8 of 33** payloads, so 76% of sessions get no
verification command at all and improvise one.

**Fair:** the derived command is tool output computed from the repo, same class as a ranked hit.
Ships no instruction; the baseline is untouched.

**Expected: +0.5% to +1.5%.** Stated honestly — 22 avoided env-failures × ~39.5K tok ≈ 0.6% of
the pool. This is a real mechanism with a small effect, not a headline.

### 5.3 Ship: R-A zero-toll delivery *(built, gated, deployed)*

Already committed (`b669a57b`) and deployed. `EG_PREFETCH=1` injected the payload into turn 0 and
still let the agent re-derive it at full price; `EG_PRESEARCH` makes the residual call an echo
(0.02 s vs 5.21 s, byte-identical). Removes 94 calls × 1.61 msgs.

**Expected +4.3% to +6.0%** (counterfactual on all 49 pairs; CI spans zero at n=49).

### 5.4 Do NOT build the post-edit hook without a decision

It is the only mechanism reaching the 97.7%, but it requires `CC_NO_SAFE_MODE=1` and a change to
patch collection (`.claude/settings.json` would land in the graded patch). It also carries the
§3 regression risk directly. Decide fairness and patch-collection acceptability first.

---

## 6. Gates — mechanism counts, winners protected

MDE is ~25–30 pts at n≈30 against a ~100-pt same-instance noise floor. **No token claim below
n≈50, in either direction.**

| gate | n | criterion |
|---|---|---|
| **V0** offline, $0 | 0 | probe returns a runnable command on cargo/pytest/phpunit/gotest/mvn repos; VERIFY coverage ≥ 80% of payloads (from 8/33); zero regressions on existing verbs |
| **V1** replay, $0 | 49 | on recorded loser sessions, the probed command would have succeeded where the emitted one failed |
| **V2** live | 12 | **harness ENV failures per session fall vs rep50**; throwaway scripts do not rise. Mechanism counts only |
| **V3** live | 50 | first token claim, bootstrap CI, total **and** median |

**Winner-protection tripwire, binding at every gate:** `lombok-3674`, `fmt-2457`,
`qutebrowser-c580`, `redis-11510` are included in every sample from V2 on. If any shows a rise in
post-edit harness runs or turns versus its rep50 record, the change is reverted regardless of the
loser-group result. lombok alone is 29% of all lift — losing it costs more than repairing the
five worst losers gains.

**Kill criteria.** V1 under 50% → the probe does not address the observed failures; stop.
V2 without a fall in env-failures → mechanism absent; stop. Any winner regression >10pt → revert.

---

## 7. Verification

- Tool: `cd /Users/suhaan/devenv/entire-graph && mise run check` (fmt + vet + race tests + build;
  CGO required for tree-sitter). Add unit tests for the probe beside `search_verify.go`.
- Offline replay: recorded queries at `results/<tag>/eg/<instance>/gq_calls.log`, payloads at the
  same path + `.payload`. Replay against the binary at zero model cost and assert both that the
  probe changes the emitted command *and* that nothing else moved.
- Harness deploys to VMs by temp path + atomic `mv` only, with a live-session guard — never
  overwrite a script a session is reading.
- Every gate reports total **and** median **and** Δturns **and** harness/env-failure counts.

---

## 8. What to tell stakeholders

The defensible claim is **not** a token saving. On Opus the tool is centrally neutral
(+1.35%, t=−0.17; −0.26% winsorised). What it demonstrably does at n=49 is suppress whole-file
reads — 119 → 105 calls, median 5,125 → 4,081 B, >8 KB tail 39 → 25 — and that is measurable now
without another cell. Report that, plus the interval on tokens, and stop quoting a percentage the
data does not support.

const FINDINGS = {
  type: 'object', additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['lens', 'findings'],
  properties: {
    lens: { type: 'string' },

    refuted: { type: 'boolean' },
    reason: { type: 'string' },
    corrected_action: { type: 'string' },
  },
}

const results = await pipeline(
  LENSES,
  (l) => agent(l.prompt, { label: `read:${l.key}`, phase: 'Read', schema: FINDINGS, effort: 'high' }),
  (r, l) => {
    if (!r || !r.findings) return { lens: l.key, headline: null, kept: [] }
    const worth = r.findings.filter((f) => f.confidence !== 'low')

)

log(`${survivors.length} findings survived refutation; ${killed.length} killed`)

  `${FACTS}\n\n` +
  `Four read-only audits ran (ledger+memory, plan documents, tool source, benchmark harness). ` +
  `Every finding was put to an adversarial refuter that defaults to refuted.\n\n` +
  `LENS HEADLINES: ${JSON.stringify(all.map((r) => ({ lens: r.lens, headline: r.headline })))}\n\n` +
  `SURVIVED: ${JSON.stringify(survivors)}\n\n` +
  `KILLED: ${JSON.stringify(killed.map((f) => ({ claim: f.claim, why: f.verdict.reason })))}\n\n` +
  `Write the decision document. The user's constraint is Opus-only, fair, best token outcome. ` +
  `Answer plainly:\n` +
  `1. On Opus, does entire-graph save tokens? Give the number and the estimator, and say whether ` +
  `the answer changes with the estimator (total +1.35%, median -4.16%, trimmed -7.65%, LOO spans zero).\n` +

  `4. What must be corrected in the existing documents and memory because it is now known wrong?\n` +
  `5. What should be STOPPED entirely?\n` +
  `Be concrete, cite measured numbers, and do not restate anything already in the closed list as if new.`,
  { label: 'decision', phase: 'Decide', effort: 'high' },
)

return { survivors, killed_count: killed.length, decision }

content.text:
Sure — here's the whole picture, plainly.

## What "the payload" is

When the agent runs `entire graph search "..."`, the tool prints a block of text: ranked hits, each with `file:line`, a score, and usually the source of the matching function. That block is **the payload**. It gets pasted into the conversation as the tool's result.

Typical sizes in this benchmark:

| thing the agent receives | median size | ≈ tokens |
|---|---|---|
| graph payload | 1,124 B | ~280 |
| a `grep` result | 732 B | ~183 |
| a **whole-file `Read`** | 5,125 B | ~1,280 |
| a big whole-file `Read` (p90) | 20,181 B | ~5,000 |

Note the graph's payload is *bigger* than a typical grep. That's why "replace grep with the graph" doesn't automatically save anything.

## How tokens get charged

A session is ~54 turns. On each turn the model is sent **the entire conversation so far** — the prompt, plus every tool result received up to that point. So:

- **95.5%** of all tokens billed are `cache_read` — re-reading context that already exists
- 3.0% is `cache_creation`, 1.5% is `output` (what the model actually writes)

This is the crucial part: **you don't pay for a tool result once. You pay for it on every turn that follows.**

## Why that changes everything

A result injected at turn 10 of a 54-turn session is re-charged ~44 more times. So its true cost is roughly:

```
cost ≈ (bytes ÷ 4) × turns_remaining
```

I call that a **persist-token**. Measured across the baseline arm's 38.6M persist-tokens:

| what | calls | cost each | share of total |
|---|---|---|---|
| exploration (grep/ls/sed/cat) | 1,206 | 14k | **45%** |
| **whole-file `Read`** | **119** | **98k** | **30%** |
| harness runs (tests/builds) | 576 | 7k | 11% |

**119 whole-file reads cost as much as 1,206 greps.** One whole-file read is 7× a grep, because it's both bigger *and* sits in context for the rest of the session.

## So how does a graph call pay for itself?

Three ways, and only three:

1. **It replaces something bigger** — one 280-token payload instead of a 1,280-token file read. Real, and it's the one place eg measurably works: whole-file reads fell 119 → 105 and their median size fell 5,125 → 4,081 B.
2. **It removes a turn** — fewer messages means less context re-read by everything after.
3. **It gets the fix right sooner** — no edit→test→fix loop.

And the cost side: the call itself is a turn, and its payload then persists. Measured, **one graph call prices at ~1.61 messages**, and a regression holding call-count fixed charges **+7.0%** for merely having made the call.

## What actually happened on Opus

- 94 graph calls made, costing ~151 messages
- they eliminated ~26 exploration calls and 31 harness runs
- net: eg spent **38 more turns** than baseline
- but each turn was **2.7% cheaper** (less junk in context)
- those nearly cancel → **+1.35%**, which is one instance away from negative

That's the whole thing: **the graph is paying a turn to buy context that's slightly cleaner, and the two roughly cancel.** It's context-neutral overall — 38.5M vs 38.6M persist-tokens.

Which is exactly why "make the losers behave like winners" is the right target you named: in losers the payload buys nothing (post-edit exploration +159), while in winners it buys convergence (−81). Same tool, opposite outcome — and the two investigators are digging into precisely why right now.

DEFECT 2 — ON "ADD" TASKS THE GRAPH RETURNS A CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER.
Search always returns something. When the task is to ADD behaviour that does not exist yet, the
top hit is plausible and wrong, and the agent follows it.
  pooled MOD (fix existing broken code) +14.35% (n=36) vs ADD -3.37% (n=21); same sign 4/4 cells,
  ~17.7pt gap, across both models and both prompts.
  Corroborating: gold at rank 2-3 measures -85.3%, WORSE than gold not found at all (-25.6%).
  Worst instance in the whole campaign is a pure ADD (fluentd "add_tag_prefix parameter", -263.6%).

WHAT IS BLOCKED, and why this is not simply "abstention":
  - Routing on the gold patch is ANSWER LEAKAGE. Forbidden.
  - A keyword classifier over the problem statement scores 57.5% against a 56% base rate, ADD
    recall 0.10. Useless.
  - Confidence / score-gap gating was tried and STRUCK: abstention measured worse. Read
    TokensNotes.md section 2.8 for exactly what was tried, and do not re-propose that same thing.
  - BUT TokensNotes.md section 3.1 records an untried idea: "a structural signal -- does the issue
    name an existing symbol that resolves in the graph? This is appealing because the graph itself
    can answer it." And section 3.3 asks whether the ADD penalty is avoidable rather than routable.

YOUR JOB:
1. Read TokensNotes.md sections 1.1, 2.8, 3.1, 3.3 and state precisely what was tried and why it
   failed, so your proposal is not a rerun.
2. Build and TEST the structural signal offline, at zero model cost: for each of the 49 rep50
   instances, extract identifiers from the problem statement, resolve them against that instance's
   graph symbol table (graphs/<iid>/graph.symbols.ndjson on the VM), and compute a resolve-rate.
   Then test whether resolve-rate separates MOD from ADD, and whether it predicts the token
   outcome. Report AUC or an equivalent, and the base rate. BE HONEST if it does not separate.
3. If the signal works, design what the TOOL does with it — remembering that abstention is struck
   and that anything the agent must read costs persist-tokens. Consider: does the answer change
   shape, shrink, or say something different? What is the cheapest expression of "the thing you
   describe does not exist here" that is tool output rather than advice?
4. Fairness argument in the required form, and the honest expected effect with an interval.
5. Kill criterion: what offline result would mean this is dead?` },

  {
    key: 'verify',
    prompt: `${BASE}

DEFECT 3 — THE VERIFY-REPAIR SPIRAL, POST-EDIT, WHERE THE TOOL IS ABSENT.
  losers vs baseline: harness ENV failures +22, throwaway scripts run +16, post-edit harness +50,
  post-edit exploration +159. Winners show the mirror: -45, -48, -88, -81.
  corr(delta env-failures, saving) = -0.442; corr(delta harness runs, saving) = -0.612.
  Chain: the verification command fails on the ENVIRONMENT rather than on the patch -> the agent
  improvises a throwaway harness -> then re-explores to repair that.
  Ledger section 1.3 (LIVE, not struck): an extra throwaway harness costs +39,527 tok/call,
  CI [+16.5K, +63.7K], stable to drop-10, negative in 3/4 cells. "The lever is giving the agent a
  verification command that actually RUNS, so it does not improvise one. A VERIFY command that
  fails on the environment rather than the patch sends the agent into 20-34 post-edit repair calls."

WHAT EXISTS TODAY:
  internal/sem/search_verify.go derives a VERIFY command and prints it in the search payload.
  Its ONLY runnability check is exec.LookPath on the runner (~line 1526) -- it confirms pytest is
  installed, it never confirms the command RUNS.
  VERIFY appears in only 8 of 33 logged payloads, so ~76% of sessions get no command at all.
  internal/cli/verify.go has a full executing verify verb with 6 ecosystem parsers -- but exposing
  an executing verb changes the claim from "does a code graph save tokens" to "does a bundle of
  dev tools save tokens", and an external reviewer already called that out. Treat shipping the
  executing verb as OUT OF SCOPE; this defect is about the DERIVED COMMAND being correct.

YOUR JOB:
1. Read internal/sem/search_verify.go end to end. Document how the command is derived, every rung
   of the fallback ladder, and exactly where it can emit something that will not run.
2. Design a COLLECT-ONLY PROBE that validates the derived command without running the suite
   (pytest --collect-only -q, go test -run XXX -count=0, cargo test --no-run, mvn -q -DskipTests
   compile, phpunit --list-tests, rspec --dry-run). Specify where it hooks in, its timeout, and
   the fallback when the probe fails. Cite file:line.
3. Measure the size of the prize offline: on the VM, for the 25 losing instances, count post-edit
   harness runs whose result text contains an ENVIRONMENT failure (command not found, module not
   found, no such file, cannot find) rather than a test failure. Then estimate turns removed if
   those had been prevented, and convert to a token effect via the persist model. Give an interval.
4. Separately assess raising VERIFY coverage from 8/33 toward 100%: what fraction of instances can
   have a command derived at all, and does emitting one where none exists today risk making things
   WORSE (an unrunnable command is worse than no command).
5. Fairness argument in the required form, plus a kill criterion.` },
]

const SPEC = {
  type: 'object', additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['defect', 'verdict', 'proposal', 'expected_pct_low', 'expected_pct_high', 'fair', 'kill_criterion'],
  properties: {
    defect: { type: 'string' },
    verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['build', 'build-with-changes', 'do-not-build'] },
    proposal: { type: 'string', description: 'Concrete change, with file:line' },
    offline_evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'What was actually measured, with numbers' },
    expected_pct_low: { type: 'number' },
    expected_pct_high: { type: 'number' },
    fair: { type: 'boolean' },
    fairness_argument: { type: 'string' },
    kill_criterion: { type: 'string' },
    risk_to_winners: { type: 'string' },
  },
}

const VERDICT = {
  type: 'object', additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['refuted', 'reason'],
  properties: {
    refuted: { type: 'boolean' },
    reason: { type: 'string' },
    revised_low: { type: 'number' },
    revised_high: { type: 'number' },
  },
}

const designed = await pipeline(
  DEFECTS,
  (d) => agent(d.prompt, { label: `design:${d.key}`, phase: 'Design', schema: SPEC, effort: 'high' }),
  (spec, d) => {
    if (!spec) return null
    return parallel([
      () => agent(`${BASE}\n\nPROPOSAL for defect "${d.key}":\n${JSON.stringify(spec, null, 1)}\n\n` +
        `REFUTE ON MECHANISM AND COST. eg is CONTEXT-NEUTRAL (38.5M vs 38.6M persist-tokens) -- there is no slack. ` +
        `Does this add bytes? Price them with the persist model and net them against the claimed benefit. ` +
        `Does it actually remove TURNS, or only change what is inside a turn? Twelve payload-quality levers died ` +
        `exactly that way. Default refuted=true unless you can trace which specific calls stop happening.`,
        { label: `refute-cost:${d.key}`, phase: 'Validate', schema: VERDICT, effort: 'high' }),
      () => agent(`${BASE}\n\nPROPOSAL for defect "${d.key}":\n${JSON.stringify(spec, null, 1)}\n\n` +
        `REFUTE ON FAIRNESS AND WINNER REGRESSION. Apply the no-tool-arm test literally. Then: winners win by ` +
        `CONVERGING (post-edit exploration -81, harness -88, turns -258) and lombok-3674 alone is 29% of all lift ` +
        `(+6.09 of +21.21 pts), where the BASELINE ran javac 70x against eg's 23x. Could this proposal make winners ` +
        `do MORE work, or help the baseline more than eg? Default refuted=true.`,
        { label: `refute-fair:${d.key}`, phase: 'Validate', schema: VERDICT, effort: 'high' }),
      () => agent(`${BASE}\n\nPROPOSAL for defect "${d.key}":\n${JSON.stringify(spec, null, 1)}\n\n` +
        `REFUTE ON MEASURABILITY AND PRIOR ART. Is the claimed effect larger than the ~100pt same-instance noise ` +
        `floor, and what n would demonstrate it (paired sd is 0.494; +6% needs 499 pairs)? Separately: open ` +
        `TokensNotes.md and confirm this is not already in the STRUCK list under another name. This project has ` +
        `retracted a dozen findings by re-proposing a dead lever with new words. Default refuted=true.`,
        { label: `refute-prior:${d.key}`, phase: 'Validate', schema: VERDICT, effort: 'high' }),
    ]).then((votes) => {
      const live = votes.filter(Boolean)
      const kills = live.filter((v) => v.refuted).length
      const lows = live.map((v) => v.revised_low).filter((n) => typeof n === 'number')
      const highs = live.map((v) => v.revised_high).filter((n) => typeof n === 'number')
      return {
        ...spec,
        survives: live.length > 0 && kills < 2,
        kills,
        votes: live.map((v) => ({ refuted: v.refuted, reason: v.reason })),
        consensus_low: lows.length ? Math.min(...lows) : spec.expected_pct_low,
        consensus_high: highs.length ? Math.max(...highs) : spec.expected_pct_high,
      }
    })
  },
)

const specs = designed.filter(Boolean)
const live = specs.filter((s) => s.survives)
log(`${live.length}/${specs.length} proposals survived 3-way adversarial refutation`)

phase('Spec')

const final = await agent(
  `${BASE}\n\n` +
  `Three defects were each given a designer and then three adversarial refuters (cost/mechanism, ` +
  `fairness/winner-regression, measurability/prior-art), each defaulting to refuted. A proposal ` +
  `survives only if fewer than 2 of 3 refuted it.\n\n` +
  `ALL PROPOSALS WITH VERDICTS:\n${JSON.stringify(specs, null, 1)}\n\n` +
  `Write the implementation spec. It must contain, for each surviving proposal:\n` +
  `  - exact files and functions to change, with file:line\n` +
  `  - the change itself, precisely enough to implement without re-deriving it\n` +
  `  - the offline ($0) validation that must pass BEFORE any cell is spent\n` +
  `  - honest expected effect WITH an interval, and the n required to demonstrate it\n` +
  `  - the fairness argument in the required form\n` +
  `  - a winner-protection tripwire (lombok-3674, fmt-2457, qutebrowser-c580, redis-11510 are ` +
  `    included in every sample; abort on >10pt regression per the user's instruction)\n` +
  `Then state plainly: summing the surviving proposals, what is the expected result on Opus, and ` +
  `does it eliminate the -19.86 pt drag pool (the user's actual goal) or not? If the honest answer ` +
  `is that it does not, say so and say what the residual is. Do not restate anything from the ` +
  `CLOSED list as if it were new.`,
  { label: 'implementation-spec', phase: 'Spec', effort: 'high' },
)

return { live_count: live.length, specs, final }

input.description: Find capabilities to add to the graph
input.prompt:
READ-ONLY architecture review. Do not modify any file. Caveman-ultra compressed output — dense bullets, file:line, numbers. Use RTK where it saves tokens.

TASK: entire-graph is a local, deterministic code-graph CLI (Go + tree-sitter, no network, no model). Read its source and tell me WHAT CAPABILITY IT SHOULD HAVE THAT IT DOES NOT — specifically capabilities that would reduce the number of TURNS a coding agent spends on a SWE-bench-style bug fix.

SOURCE: /Users/suhaan/devenv/entire-graph
  internal/sem/    parsing, graph construction, search  (provider.go, search.go, search_verify.go, search_related.go, dependents.go)
  internal/cli/    hand-rolled dispatch (root.go, search.go, def.go, impact.go, neighbors.go, changed.go, verify.go, callsite.go)
  internal/gitutil/ git subprocess helpers
  docs/adr/        contracts
  AGENTS.md        the shipped operating doctrine

START HERE, these are load-bearing:
  `entire-graph capabilities --json` lists semantic vs inventory-only languages, relation types, features.
  30 relation types exist (CALLS, IMPORTS, EXTENDS, HANDLES_ROUTE, USES_TYPE, PARAM_TYPE,
  RETURNS_TYPE, DATA_FLOWS, FILE_CHANGES_WITH, CONTAINS, ...).

KNOWN DEAD ENDS — a proposal that reduces to any of these is worthless, say so and move on:
  - a new VERB advertised in the prompt's affordance tail. Measured adoption 0/66 across three
    attempts (impact 0/49, changed 0/5, --path 0/12). The agent does not reach for new verbs.
  - anything requiring a graph call AFTER the first edit: 42/49 sessions make none.
  - better ranking: sessions where the gold file ranked FIRST lost more often than sessions where
    it was missed entirely. Retrieval quality and token cost are different axes.
  - bigger or richer payloads: the tool is already CONTEXT-NEUTRAL (38.5M vs 38.6M persist-weighted
    tokens vs the no-tool baseline). Every added byte is spent from a zero balance. Twelve
    payload-quality metrics have been measured and all are dead, including complete-symbol density
    (correlates -0.170 with token saving).

THE COST MODEL you must price against:
  cache_read is 95.5% of billed tokens. A tool result injected at turn i is re-charged on every
  later turn, so cost ~= (bytes/4) x turns-remaining ("persist-tokens").
  Baseline session cost by class: exploration 45.1% (1,206 calls x 14k), whole-file Read 30.3%
  (only 119 calls but 98k EACH - 7x anything else), harness runs 11.2% (576 x 7k).
  Median sizes: graph payload 1,124 B, grep 732 B, whole-file Read 5,125 B (p90 20,181 B).
  A graph call prices at 1.61 messages.
  => The single most valuable thing a capability can do is PREVENT A WHOLE-FILE READ or REMOVE A
     TURN. Adding bytes to prevent nothing is negative.

CORPUS: SWE-bench Multilingual. ~48% dynamically typed (Ruby 39, PHP 32, JS 23, TS 8) vs typed
(Java 31, Rust 31, Go 27, C 22). Any capability relying on static types works on ~half at best.

DELIVER:
1. A CAPABILITY INVENTORY: what the graph computes today but never surfaces to the agent, or
   surfaces only behind an unset flag / a verb nobody calls. The project has repeatedly found
   capabilities that shipped and were never wired up — find the rest. file:line for each.
2. For each of the 30 relation types: is it populated (roughly how many edges on a real repo), and
   is it reachable by the agent? Flag any that are computed and thrown away. Known example to
   verify: TESTS reportedly has ~10 edges out of ~36,000 and is name-convention only.
3. THE MAIN ASK — 3 to 6 NEW capabilities, ranked by (turns removed) / (bytes added). For each:
     - the question the agent is actually trying to answer when it burns turns
     - the exact command and output shape
     - why the graph can answer it and grep cannot
     - which of the dead ends above it avoids, and how it reaches the agent WITHOUT being a new
       verb in the affordance tail
     - honest byte cost and turn saving
4. Anything in the DEFAULT behaviour that is actively harmful given the cost model — e.g. defaults
   that inflate payload size, or `search --profile fast` reportedly excluding TESTS/SIMILAR_TO/all
   type relations/DATA_FLOWS/FILE_CHANGES_WITH so those blocks come back structurally empty.
5. Be blunt: if the honest conclusion is that no new capability clears the bar because the tool is
   context-neutral and the agent will not call new things, say that and explain what that implies
   about the product.

Here's how the graph actually works, measured on this repo (36,359 edges, 7,370 symbols). ## The pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph BUILD["BUILD — deterministic, local, no network, no model"] A["repo working tree"] --> B["tree-sitter parse
205 file extensions"] B --> C{"language tier"} C -->|"36 semantic langs
Go Rust Java Py Rb PHP TS…"| D["full extraction:
symbols + 30 relation types"] C -->|"149 inventory-only
ABAP, Awk, BASIC…"| E["symbols only:
CONTAINS + DEFINES"] D --> F["graph: 7,370 symbols
36,359 edges"] E --> F F --> G["gzip snapshot cache
keyed by tree hash"] end subgraph QUERY["QUERY — what the agent calls"] G --> H["search --query
hybrid rank"] G --> I["def / neighbors / impact
changed / grep"] H --> J["payload: ranked hits
file:line + source
median 1,124 B"] I --> J end J --> K["agent's context
re-charged EVERY later turn"] ``` ## There are no custom groups or per-repo rules This is the part worth being clear about: **the same code path runs for every repo.** No per-repo config, no per-language principles, no tuned profiles. | bucket | eg | base | Δ |

Hard delivery constraint I worked under: **both sessions made exactly one graph call, pre-edit, and never returned.** So the only channel that reaches anyone is the *first `entire graph search` response*. **Confirmed — both claims check out.**

**1. `entire graph grep` has no vendor/minified/generated filtering.** It shells out to plain `grep -rInE` over the whole worktree and filters only tests (`istest`). So on prometheus it returned one hit inside minified vendored `d3.v3.js` where plain grep returned a clean zero. That inversion is the defect: **a clean zero is actionable** ("this doesn't exist, pivot"), **one noise hit is not** — it invites confirmation greps. Baseline pivoted to the error string at call 2 and found `scalarBinop`; eg reached it at calls 21–22. **~19 turns of delay seeded by the tool's opening answer.**

This is the first defect all session where the graph is *demonstrably worse than no tool at all*, and the fix **removes bytes** rather than adding them.

**2. Validation is clean:**

| check | result |
|---|---|
| graphs present, commit-matched | **49/49, 0 mismatches** |
| graphs under 50 KB (extraction failure) | **0** of 310 |
| cache dirs | 2, small — no staleness risk |
| prompt symmetry | 18 differing lines, **all checkout paths** — expected and symmetric |
| binaries in logs | 3 distinct shas across cells — rep50 used `8daf183ee29d` |

**3. Two integrity findings to fold in:**
- **Shared `/tmp` leaks between concurrent cells.** prometheus-eg found `/tmp/goyacc`, `/tmp/goyacc-build/goyacc` built by *other* instances' sessions and spent 2 calls auditing foreign binaries. That fabricates per-instance deltas.
- **`EG_LITERALS` is built and was OFF in this cell.** The error-literal→symbol index would have collapsed prometheus's biggest delay — the capability exists and was disabled.

**Also material:** both these losers are **ADD tasks**, and **80%/64% of their surplus is PRE-EDIT** — the opposite of the corpus-level "97.7% post-edit". So the graph doesn't get the "absent at the scene" defence on them; it bled where it operates.
